subdomainName: Identify and Classify Information and Assets
title: Government classification levels and damage criteria
prompt: Order the US government classification levels from highest to lowest and state the damage each one implies if disclosed.
answerSummary: Top Secret: exceptionally grave damage. Secret: serious damage. Confidential: damage. Unclassified: no damage to national security (CUI is a separate unclassified category that still needs safeguarding).
mnemonic: Grave → Serious → Damage → None. Top Secret is the only one with "exceptionally grave".
examTrapWarning: Confidential is the lowest classified level, not the highest. "Serious damage" is Secret, not Top Secret.

steps.label: Top Secret
steps.detail: Unauthorized disclosure could cause exceptionally grave damage to national security.

steps.label: Secret
steps.detail: Unauthorized disclosure could cause serious damage.

steps.label: Unclassified
steps.detail: Not classified; Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) still requires handling controls.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identify and Classify Information and Assets
title: Commercial vs. government classification equivalents
prompt: Map the common commercial classification labels to their approximate government equivalents.
answerSummary: Confidential/Proprietary ≈ Top Secret, Private ≈ Secret, Sensitive ≈ Confidential, Public ≈ Unclassified.
examTrapWarning: "Confidential" means different things: in commercial schemes it is the highest level, in the government scheme it is the lowest classified level.

rows: Employee PII, HR and salary records

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identify and Classify Information and Assets
title: FIPS 199 high-water mark
prompt: Fill in how FIPS 199 sets a system's overall impact level.
answerSummary: FIPS 199 rates confidentiality, integrity and availability impact as Low, Moderate or High; the system's overall category takes the highest rating (high-water mark).
examTrapWarning: Do not average the three ratings. One High rating makes the whole system High.
clozeTemplate: FIPS 199 rates each of confidentiality, integrity and availability as {{c1::Low, Moderate or High::three levels}}. The system's overall impact level follows the {{c2::high-water mark::rule}}: the {{c3::highest::which rating}} of the three.

references.section: Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems

topicName: Data Owner vs. Data Controller vs. Data Processor
title: Data controller vs. processor vs. custodian
prompt: Contrast the GDPR data controller and data processor with the internal data custodian role.
answerSummary: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and carries primary accountability. The processor handles data only on the controller's documented instructions (for example a cloud payroll provider). The custodian is an internal technical role that implements protections the owner requires.
examTrapWarning: A cloud provider following your instructions is a processor; you remain the controller and stay accountable for the breach notification.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Controller decides purpose and means; processor follows instructions; custodian implements controls.

columns.label: Data controller
points: Determines purposes and means of processing

columns.label: Data processor
points: Bound by a data processing agreement
Must notify the controller of breaches

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

title: Anonymization vs. pseudonymization vs. tokenization vs. masking
prompt: Contrast the four data de-identification techniques: reversible or not, and their regulatory effect.
answerSummary: Anonymization is irreversible, so the data falls outside GDPR. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with aliases that can be re-linked using separately held data, so it is still personal data. Tokenization swaps sensitive values for random tokens stored in a vault, reducing PCI DSS scope. Masking hides part of a value (e.g., ****1234) for display or testing.
examTrapWarning: Pseudonymized data is still personal data under GDPR. Only true anonymization removes it from scope.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Only anonymization is irreversible; the other three can be reversed or still identify someone.

columns.label: Tokenization
points: Original stored in a secure token vault

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Media Sanitization (NIST SP 800-88: Clear, Purge, Destroy, Cryptographic Erase)
title: NIST SP 800-88: Clear vs. Purge vs. Destroy
prompt: Define the three NIST SP 800-88 sanitization levels, the techniques for each, and the recovery they defeat.
answerSummary: Clear: logical techniques (overwrite) that defeat simple, non-invasive recovery. Purge: physical or logical techniques (degauss, block erase, cryptographic erase) that defeat state-of-the-art lab recovery. Destroy: shred, disintegrate, pulverize, melt or incinerate so the media cannot be reused.
mnemonic: C-P-D grows in strength: Clean the surface, Purge the lab-recoverable, Destroy the media.
examTrapWarning: Purged media can be reused; destroyed media cannot. Leaving the organization or a lower classification usually requires purge or destroy, not clear.

rows: Overwrite with non-sensitive data, factory reset

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Media Sanitization (NIST SP 800-88: Clear, Purge, Destroy, Cryptographic Erase)
title: Retiring SSDs that held sensitive data
prompt: A technician plans to degauss a pallet of laptops with SSDs before donating them. What should happen instead?
answerSummary: Degaussing does nothing to flash storage. Use cryptographic erase or the vendor's sanitize command (purge) and verify, or physically destroy drives that held highly sensitive data, in line with the media sanitization policy.
examTrapWarning: Overwriting an SSD also fails because wear leveling leaves stale blocks behind. Degaussing is only for magnetic media such as HDDs and tapes.

heuristicData.technicalReflexTrap: Degauss the SSDs or run a multi-pass overwrite and assume the data is gone.
heuristicData.managerAction: Follow the sanitization policy: use cryptographic erase or firmware sanitize (purge) with verification and a certificate, or destroy the drives if data sensitivity requires it.
heuristicData.governingPrinciple: Sanitization must match the media type and data sensitivity (NIST SP 800-88), and be documented.

title: How long to keep records
prompt: Fill in the principle that sets record retention periods.
answerSummary: Keep data only as long as laws, regulations or business needs require, then dispose of it securely. Keeping it longer adds cost, breach exposure and eDiscovery liability. A legal hold suspends normal destruction.
examTrapWarning: "Keep everything forever" is wrong: excess data increases liability and discovery costs.
clozeTemplate: Records should be kept only as long as required by {{c1::law, regulation or business need::drivers}}, then securely destroyed. Over-retention increases {{c2::liability and eDiscovery exposure::risk}}, and a {{c3::legal hold::litigation mechanism}} overrides the normal destruction schedule.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Data Security Controls & States of Data
topicName: Data at Rest, Data in Transit, Data in Use
title: The three states of data and their controls
prompt: Name the three data states and the main protections for each.
answerSummary: At rest: storage encryption (full-disk, database TDE) and access control. In transit: TLS, IPsec, SSH. In use: memory protections, trusted execution environments (confidential computing) and homomorphic encryption.
examTrapWarning: Data in use is the hardest to protect because it is normally decrypted in memory. TLS does nothing for data sitting on a disk.

rows: AES full-disk encryption, TDE, access control
TEEs / secure enclaves, memory encryption, homomorphic encryption

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Data Security Controls & States of Data
title: Network DLP vs. endpoint DLP vs. CASB
prompt: Contrast where network DLP, endpoint DLP and a CASB inspect data and what each can stop.
answerSummary: Network DLP inspects traffic at the egress point (email, web) but cannot see encrypted traffic without TLS inspection or USB copies. Endpoint DLP runs on the device and can block USB, printing and clipboard copies. A CASB sits between users and cloud services to enforce policy on SaaS use, including shadow IT.
examTrapWarning: Network DLP cannot stop a user copying files to a USB stick; that needs endpoint DLP.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Pick the DLP placement that sees the channel the data leaves through.

columns.label: Network DLP
points: Inspects email, web and file transfers
Blind to encrypted traffic without TLS inspection

columns.label: CASB
points: Between users and SaaS / cloud apps

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Marking, Labeling, Storage, and Secure Transport of Sensitive Media
title: Labeling combined information
prompt: Fill in the labeling rule for media containing information of several classification levels.
answerSummary: Media or documents holding mixed data are labeled at the highest classification present, and the label must be visible to humans (marking) and readable by systems (labels/metadata).
examTrapWarning: Aggregated low-level data can itself become more sensitive than any single item; review the combined set's classification.
clozeTemplate: When a document or drive holds information of several classifications, it is marked at the {{c1::highest::level}} classification it contains. Combining many lower-level items can raise sensitivity, a problem called {{c2::aggregation::term}}.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Marking, Labeling, Storage, and Secure Transport of Sensitive Media
title: Scheduled destruction vs. a pending lawsuit
prompt: Backups are due for routine destruction next week, but legal counsel has just warned of pending litigation involving that data. What do you do?
answerSummary: Suspend destruction of the relevant data under a legal hold as directed by counsel. Destroying it could be spoliation of evidence, even if it follows the normal schedule.
examTrapWarning: Following the retention schedule "because it is policy" is wrong once a legal hold applies.

heuristicData.technicalReflexTrap: Destroy the backups on schedule because the retention policy says so.
heuristicData.managerAction: Work with legal counsel to place a legal hold, preserve the relevant data and pause the destruction schedule for it until counsel releases the hold.
heuristicData.governingPrinciple: Legal holds override retention schedules; destroying relevant data during litigation is spoliation.
